areas.title: Programming language
areas.question: Which language should this be written in?

needs.web-full-stack: One language for browser and server
needs.hiring: Easy to find people who know it

options.name: Rust
options.summary: Compiled, memory-safe without a garbage collector; fast and predictable.
pros: Speed close to C and C++ with memory safety checked at compile time
One self-contained binary; no runtime to install
Strong types and a helpful compiler catch many bugs before they run
cons: Slower to learn and to write at first
Fewer people know it than Python or TypeScript
guide: Install Rust with rustup from rust-lang.org
Run `cargo new <name>` to create the project
Run `cargo build` and `cargo test` to check it builds
Add dependencies with `cargo add <crate>`

checks.why: A binary or service builds the same versions everywhere only with its lock file committed.

options.name: TypeScript (Node.js)
options.summary: JavaScript with types; runs in the browser and on the server.
pros: One language for the browser and the server
Huge package ecosystem and many developers
Types catch mistakes while staying quick to write
cons: Slower and hungrier for memory than compiled languages
Dependency trees grow large and need care
Types are checked at build time only, not at run time
guide: Install Node.js (LTS) from nodejs.org
Run `npm init -y` and `npm install --save-dev typescript`
Run `npx tsc --init` to create tsconfig.json
Add a build script to package.json and run it

checks.why: Without package-lock.json (or pnpm's or yarn's), each install may pull different versions.
strict catches null and type mistakes the default settings let through.

options.name: Python
options.summary: Readable, quick to write, with the strongest data and machine-learning ecosystem.
pros: The leading ecosystem for data and machine learning
cons: Slower than compiled languages for CPU-heavy work
Types are optional hints unless a checker is run
guide: Install Python 3 from python.org
Create a virtual environment: `python -m venv .venv`
Describe the project and its dependencies in pyproject.toml
Install them into the environment and run the tests

checks.why: pyproject.toml alone allows newer versions on each install; a lock file (uv, Poetry, PDM) pins what was tested.

options.name: Go
options.summary: Simple compiled language built for network services.
pros: Simple language that teams pick up quickly
Fast builds and one static binary
cons: Less expressive types than Rust or TypeScript
Garbage collected, so less predictable than Rust under tight memory
Smaller ecosystem for data and machine learning
guide: Install Go from go.dev
Run `go mod init <module>`
Write main.go and run `go run .`
Run `go test ./...`

options.name: Java or Kotlin (JVM)
options.summary: Mature, fast runtime with a deep enterprise ecosystem.
cons: More ceremony than Python or Go
Larger memory use and slower start-up
Build tools (Maven, Gradle) take time to learn
guide: Install a JDK (for example Eclipse Temurin)
Create the project with Gradle or Maven
Run the build and tests
Pick a framework if it is a service

options.name: C# (.NET)
options.summary: Fast, well-tooled runtime, strong on Windows and cross-platform servers.
pros: One ecosystem for desktop, web and services
Strong typing with modern language features
cons: Smaller open-source community than Node or Python
Larger deployments than Go or Rust
guide: Install the .NET SDK from dotnet.microsoft.com
Run `dotnet new <template>`
Run `dotnet build` and `dotnet test`

areas.title: Primary database
areas.question: Which database should hold the application's data?

needs.transactions: Changes that must all succeed or all fail
needs.embedded: A file inside the app, no server
needs.single-user: One user or one process writes
needs.serverless: Pay per use, scales to zero
needs.analytics: Reports and aggregates over the data

options.name: PostgreSQL
options.summary: The default relational database: reliable, featureful and widely hosted.
pros: Strong transactions and constraints keep data correct
Rich features: JSON columns, full-text search, extensions
Offered by every major cloud as a managed service
cons: A server to run, back up and upgrade (or to pay for)
Connections are costly; needs a pool under load
More than a small single-user tool needs
options.cost: Free; managed hosting is billed by size
guide: Create a database: install PostgreSQL locally, or create a managed instance with your cloud provider
Create a user and a database for the app, with a strong password
Put the connection string in the app's secret settings, not in the code
Add a migrations tool and write the first migration
Set up automatic backups and test a restore

checks.why: Each PostgreSQL connection is a process on the server; a pool reuses a few connections instead of opening one per request.
Versioned migrations make schema changes repeatable and reviewable across machines.

options.name: SQLite
options.summary: A whole SQL database in one file, inside the app.
pros: No server: one file, nothing to operate
Very fast for one process and many readers
cons: Not shared across machines without extra tools
Fewer types and features than PostgreSQL
guide: Add the SQLite driver for the language
Choose where the database file lives (outside the code folder)
Turn on write-ahead logging (`PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`)
Write the first migration and back the file up regularly

checks.why: WAL lets readers work while one writer writes, and is usually faster than the default journal.

options.name: MySQL or MariaDB
options.summary: A widely hosted relational database, common in web hosting.
pros: Available almost everywhere, including cheap hosting
Simple to operate for typical web apps
cons: Some defaults are less strict about data
options.cost: Free; managed hosting is billed by size
guide: Create a database server or a managed instance
Create a user and a database for the app
Keep the connection string in secret settings
Add migrations and set up backups

options.name: MongoDB
options.summary: A document database: records as flexible JSON-like documents.
pros: Records can change shape without migrations
A managed service (Atlas) runs it for you
cons: Joins and constraints are weaker than in SQL databases
Easy to let data drift into inconsistent shapes
Server Side Public Licence limits offering it as a service
options.cost: Free to self-host; Atlas is billed by size
guide: Create a cluster (Atlas or self-hosted)
Create a database user and allow the app's network
Keep the connection string in secret settings
Define indexes for the queries the app runs

checks.why: A schema (Mongoose, JSON Schema validation, or app-side validation) keeps documents consistent.

options.name: Firestore
options.summary: Google's serverless document database, with live updates to clients.
pros: Nothing to run; scales to zero
Live updates straight to web and mobile clients
cons: Costs grow with reads and writes, which can surprise
Ties the app to Google Cloud
guide: Create a Firebase or Google Cloud project
Create a Firestore database and choose its region
Write security rules before any client connects
Add the SDK and a service account for the server

options.name: DynamoDB
options.summary: AWS's serverless key-value and document database.
pros: Scales to very high traffic with steady latency
Integrates with the rest of AWS
cons: Queries must be designed up front around keys
Ad-hoc questions and joins are hard
guide: Design the access patterns and keys first
Create the table in the AWS console or with infrastructure code
Give the app an IAM role limited to the table
Add the AWS SDK

areas.title: Cache and fast key-value store
areas.question: Where should the app keep cached or short-lived data?

options.name: Redis or Valkey
options.summary: An in-memory store with rich data structures, shared by all servers.
pros: Very fast, shared by every server
Counters, sets, sorted sets and streams built in
Widely hosted as a managed service
cons: Another server to run or pay for
Redis's own licence changed; Valkey is the open-source fork
options.licence: BSD-3-Clause (Valkey); Redis has changed licences, check the version
options.cost: Free to self-host; managed is billed by memory
guide: Create a Redis or Valkey instance (managed or self-hosted)
Require a password and keep it in secret settings
Set a memory limit and an eviction policy
Give each kind of key an expiry

options.name: In-process cache
options.summary: A map in the app's own memory, with expiry.
cons: Each server has its own copy
guide: Pick the language's standard cache library (with a size limit and expiry)
Cache only what can be rebuilt
Measure the hit rate

options.name: Memcached
options.summary: A simple, fast, shared memory cache.
cons: Less common in new projects than Redis
guide: Run Memcached or a managed instance
Point the app's cache client at it
Keep values small and give them expiries

areas.title: File and object storage
areas.question: Where should uploaded files, images and backups live?

needs.cheap-egress: Low cost to download a lot

options.name: Amazon S3
options.summary: The reference object store; its API is the industry standard.
pros: Lifecycle rules and storage classes cut cost
cons: Permissions (IAM, bucket policies) are easy to get wrong
Ties to AWS unless the S3 API is used elsewhere
guide: Create a bucket in the region the app runs in
Block public access unless files must be public
Give the app a role or key limited to the bucket
Add lifecycle rules for old files

options.name: Google Cloud Storage
options.summary: Google Cloud's object store.
cons: Its own API (an S3-compatible mode exists but is partial)
guide: Create a bucket in the app's region
Use uniform bucket-level access
Give the app's service account access to that bucket only

options.name: Cloudflare R2
options.summary: An S3-compatible object store with no egress fees.
cons: Another provider beside the main cloud
options.cost: Usage-based: storage and requests, no egress
guide: Create an R2 bucket in the Cloudflare dashboard
Create an API token limited to that bucket
Point an S3 client at the R2 endpoint

options.name: Local disk
options.summary: Files on the server's own disk.
cons: Lost if the server's disk is lost
guide: Pick a folder outside the code and outside the web root
Back it up on a schedule
Limit upload sizes and types

areas.title: Search
areas.question: How should users search the app's content?

options.name: PostgreSQL full-text search
options.summary: Search inside the database already in use.
pros: Always in sync with the data
cons: Heavy search load shares the database
guide: Add a tsvector column (or a generated one) for the searchable text
Index it with a GIN index
Query with to_tsquery or websearch_to_tsquery

options.name: Meilisearch
options.summary: A fast, typo-tolerant search engine that is simple to run.
pros: Instant, forgiving results out of the box
cons: Another service to keep in sync
Not built for very large log-style data
Some features are in the paid cloud
options.cost: Free to self-host; cloud is paid
guide: Run Meilisearch (container or cloud)
Set a master key and keep it secret
Index the documents and keep the index updated on changes

options.name: OpenSearch or Elasticsearch
options.summary: Distributed search and analytics for very large collections.
pros: Scales to huge collections and logs
options.cost: Free to self-host; managed is billed by size
guide: Start with a managed cluster
Define the index mappings before indexing
Keep the index in sync from the database

needs.control: Own the user data and flow

options.name: Built in (a library in the app)
options.summary: The app's own sign-in with a well-known library: sessions, password hashing, OAuth.
pros: Full control of users and data
No outside service in the sign-in path
cons: Security is your responsibility (hashing, resets, rate limits)
Social and enterprise sign-in take extra work
guide: Pick a maintained auth library for the framework
Hash passwords with Argon2id or bcrypt
Add email verification and password reset
Rate-limit sign-in attempts
Add OAuth providers if wanted

checks.suggest: Hash passwords with Argon2id, bcrypt or scrypt
checks.why: A slow, salted hash is what keeps stolen password data from being reversed.

options.name: Auth0
options.summary: A hosted identity service with enterprise features.
pros: Enterprise single sign-on and many providers
cons: Costs rise with users and features
User data lives with the vendor
options.cost: Free tier; then per active user
guide: Create an Auth0 tenant and an application
Set the allowed callback and logout addresses
Add the SDK and keep the client secret in secret settings
Test sign-in, sign-out and token checks

options.name: Clerk
options.summary: Hosted sign-in with ready-made UI components for web apps.
pros: Quick to set up in React and Next.js
cons: Per-user pricing beyond the free tier
Best fit for JavaScript front ends
options.cost: Free tier; then per active user
guide: Create a Clerk application
Add the SDK and wrap the app in its provider
Keep the secret key in secret settings
Protect server routes with its middleware

options.name: Supabase Auth
options.summary: Sign-in that comes with a hosted PostgreSQL project.
pros: Works with Supabase's PostgreSQL and row-level security
cons: Best when the rest of the app uses Supabase
Enterprise sign-in is on paid plans
Self-hosting is a lot to run
guide: Create a Supabase project
Turn on the sign-in methods wanted
Use row-level security on tables
Keep the service-role key on the server only

options.name: Keycloak
options.summary: A self-hosted, open-source identity server.
pros: Full single sign-on, SAML and OIDC
guide: Run Keycloak with a PostgreSQL database
Create a realm and a client for the app
Connect the app with an OIDC library
Set up backups and upgrades

areas.title: Payments
areas.question: How should the app take payments?

needs.merchant-of-record: Someone else handles sales tax and VAT

options.name: Stripe
options.summary: The developer-first payments platform.
pros: Excellent APIs, docs and test mode
cons: You are the seller: sales tax and VAT are yours (Stripe Tax helps, for a fee)
Disputes and fraud are yours to handle
guide: Create a Stripe account and stay in test mode
Create the products and prices
Use hosted Checkout and the customer portal
Handle webhooks, verifying their signatures
Switch to live keys only after testing

checks.why: Payments complete asynchronously; a signed webhook is how the app learns of them reliably.

options.name: Paddle
options.summary: A merchant of record: it sells on your behalf and handles tax.
pros: Handles sales tax and VAT worldwide
cons: Higher fees than a plain processor
guide: Apply for a Paddle account
Create products and prices
Add Paddle's checkout
Handle its webhooks

options.name: Lemon Squeezy
options.summary: A merchant of record aimed at software and digital products.
pros: Quick to set up for digital products
cons: Higher fees than a plain processor
guide: Create a store
Add the products
Use its checkout links or overlay
Handle its webhooks

areas.title: Sending email
areas.question: Which service should send the app's email?

options.name: Amazon SES
options.summary: Very cheap email sending from AWS.
cons: Bare-bones; templates and analytics are basic
Starts in a sandbox until approved
guide: Verify your sending domain (SPF, DKIM, DMARC records)
Ask AWS to leave the sandbox
Give the app credentials limited to sending
Handle bounces and complaints

options.name: Postmark
options.summary: Transactional email focused on fast, reliable delivery.
cons: Marketing mail is a separate stream
guide: Create a server and verify the domain (SPF, DKIM)
Add the API token to secret settings
Send a test email and check its logs

options.name: Resend
options.summary: A developer-friendly email API with React email templates.
guide: Create an API key
Verify the sending domain
Send from the server only

options.name: SendGrid
options.summary: Long-standing email platform for both transactional and marketing mail.
cons: Shared sending ranges can hurt deliverability on low plans
guide: Create an API key with send permission only
Authenticate the domain
Set up a suppression list and unsubscribe handling

needs.static-site: A static or mostly static site

options.name: Container platform (Cloud Run, Fly.io, App Runner)
options.summary: Run a container; the platform scales it and gives it HTTPS.
pros: Deploy any container, no servers to patch
Scales with traffic, some scale to zero
cons: Cold starts when scaled to zero
Long-running or stateful work fits less well
Platform limits on memory and time
guide: Write a Dockerfile (small base image, non-root user)
Build and push the image to the platform's registry
Create the service, set its secrets as environment settings
Point a domain at it

checks.why: Without it, the whole folder (including secrets and build output) goes into the image's build context.

options.name: Static and edge hosting (Cloudflare Pages, Vercel, Netlify)
options.summary: Static files and small functions served from a global network.
pros: Fast everywhere, often free for small sites
Deploys from git on every push
cons: Server code limited to the platform's functions
Costs can jump at high traffic on some plans
options.cost: Free tier; then by plan and usage
guide: Connect the git repository
Set the build command and output folder
Add environment settings for secrets
Point the domain and check HTTPS

options.name: Virtual machine
options.summary: A server you run yourself (Compute Engine, EC2, a VPS).
cons: Patching, backups and security are yours
guide: Create the machine with the smallest size that fits
Lock down SSH (keys only) and the firewall
Install the app as a service that restarts
Set up automatic security updates and backups

options.name: Kubernetes
options.summary: An orchestrator for many containers across machines.
pros: Runs many services with one model
guide: Use a managed cluster
Describe each service with manifests or Helm
Add resource limits and health checks
Set up monitoring before production

areas.title: Background jobs and messaging
areas.question: How should work happen in the background or between services?

options.name: Jobs table in the database
options.summary: Background jobs stored in the database already in use.
pros: Jobs and data change in one transaction
guide: Pick a jobs library for the database and language
Create its tables with a migration
Run a worker process beside the app
Retry failed jobs with backoff

options.name: Redis-backed queue
options.summary: Job queues on Redis (BullMQ, Sidekiq, RQ, Celery).
pros: Delays, retries and priorities built in
cons: Jobs can be lost if Redis is not persisted
guide: Add the queue library
Point it at Redis
Run worker processes
Add a dashboard or alerts for failures

options.name: Managed queue (SQS, Pub/Sub)
options.summary: A cloud provider's queue or pub/sub.
guide: Create the queue or topic
Give producers and consumers limited permissions
Set a dead-letter queue for failures

options.name: Kafka
options.summary: A durable event log for high-volume streams.
guide: Use a managed Kafka service
Design topics and their retention
Add schema management for events

areas.title: Errors, logs and monitoring
areas.question: How should you learn when something breaks in production?

needs.errors: Know about errors with their context

options.name: Sentry
options.summary: Error tracking with stack traces and releases.
guide: Create a Sentry project
Add the SDK and set the DSN in settings
Turn on scrubbing of personal data
Tag releases so errors map to deploys

options.name: OpenTelemetry with Grafana
options.summary: The open standard for traces, metrics and logs, with Grafana to view them.
cons: More setup than an error tracker
Errors need dashboards and alerts built
options.cost: Free to self-host; cloud by volume
guide: Add the OpenTelemetry SDK and auto-instrumentation
Run a collector or point at a cloud endpoint
Build a dashboard and alerts for errors and latency

options.name: Datadog
options.summary: An all-in-one hosted monitoring platform.
guide: Create an account and install the agent
Add the tracing library
Set up monitors before turning on more products

areas.title: Server framework
areas.question: Which framework should the server use?

needs.batteries-included: Admin, ORM and auth built in
needs.typed-api: Typed requests and responses, generated docs
needs.jvm: The project is Java or Kotlin

options.name: Axum (Rust)
options.summary: A light, fast web framework on Tokio.
pros: Typed extractors catch mistakes at compile time
cons: Bring your own ORM, auth and admin
Fewer ready-made plug-ins than older frameworks
guide: `cargo add axum tokio --features tokio/full`
Define routes and handlers
Add tower-http for logging, CORS and compression

options.name: FastAPI (Python)
options.summary: A typed Python API framework with generated docs.
pros: Request and response types from Python type hints
cons: Bring your own ORM, auth and admin
Async and sync code mixed carelessly hurts performance
guide: Install fastapi and uvicorn
Define models with Pydantic
Run with uvicorn behind a process manager

options.name: Django (Python)
options.summary: A batteries-included Python web framework.
pros: ORM, migrations, admin and auth built in
cons: Its own way of doing things
guide: `pip install django` and `django-admin startproject`
Create apps and models, then run migrations
Use the admin for internal tools

checks.suggest: Make sure DEBUG is off in production
checks.why: Django with DEBUG on shows internal details to anyone who triggers an error.

options.name: Fastify or Express (Node.js)
options.summary: Node.js web frameworks: Fastify is faster and schema-based, Express is the long-standing default.
pros: Fastify validates with JSON schemas and is fast
Same language as the front end
cons: Bring your own structure, ORM and auth
Express is slower and less maintained than Fastify
Easy to grow messy without conventions
guide: Install fastify (or express)
Define routes with schemas
Add security headers and rate limiting

checks.why: Express sends none of the usual security headers by default; helmet adds them.

options.name: Go standard library (net/http) or chi
options.summary: Go's built-in HTTP server, with a light router if wanted.
pros: The standard library's router handles most needs
guide: Define handlers with net/http
Add chi if routes grow
Add timeouts on the server

options.name: Spring Boot (Java or Kotlin)
options.summary: The standard JVM framework for services.
guide: Generate a project at start.spring.io
Pick the starters needed
Run with the Gradle or Maven plugin

areas.title: Web front end
areas.question: How should the web interface be built?

needs.hiring: Easy to find people who know it

options.name: React (with Next.js)
options.summary: The most widely used UI library, with Next.js for routing and server rendering.
pros: Next.js adds server rendering and routing
cons: Next.js adds complexity and favours Vercel's hosting
guide: `npx create-next-app@latest`
Pick the App Router and TypeScript
Add a component library if wanted
Deploy and check the bundle size

options.name: Svelte (with SvelteKit)
options.summary: A compiler-based UI framework with small bundles.
pros: Less code than React for the same UI
guide: `npx sv create`
Choose TypeScript
Add an adapter for the hosting target

options.name: Vue (with Nuxt)
options.summary: An approachable UI framework, with Nuxt for full apps.
cons: Two styles (Options, Composition) in the wild
Fewer jobs than React in some markets
guide: `npx nuxi init`
Use the Composition API and TypeScript
Pick a hosting preset

options.name: Astro
options.summary: Content-first sites that send little or no JavaScript.
pros: Pages ship as HTML, JavaScript only where needed
Use components from React, Svelte or Vue
Great for docs, blogs and marketing
guide: `npm create astro@latest`
Write pages in .astro and content in Markdown
Add islands only where interaction is needed

options.name: Server-rendered pages with htmx
options.summary: HTML from the server, with small interactive parts.
cons: Rich, offline or very interactive UIs are hard
A different way of thinking for SPA developers
guide: Render pages with the server's templates
Add htmx with one script tag
Return HTML fragments for interactive parts

areas.title: System architecture
areas.question: How should the system be split into parts?

options.name: Modular monolith
options.summary: One deployable app, split inside into clear modules.
pros: One thing to build, test and deploy
Calls between modules are fast and simple
Can be split later along module lines
cons: Modules need discipline to stay apart
guide: Define modules by business area
Let modules talk only through their public interfaces
Keep one database, with each module owning its tables

options.name: Microservices
options.summary: Separate services, each with its own deploy and data.
pros: Each part scales on its own
cons: Network calls, versioning and tracing add complexity
Data consistency across services is hard
guide: Split only where teams or scaling truly differ
Give each service its own data
Add tracing and contracts between services from the start

options.name: Serverless functions
options.summary: Small functions run by the platform on each request or event.
cons: Hard to test and debug locally
guide: Keep each function small and stateless
Store state in a managed database
Watch cold starts and costs

areas.title: API style
areas.question: How should clients talk to the server?

needs.flexible-queries: Clients choose which data they get

options.name: REST with OpenAPI
options.summary: Resources over HTTP, described by an OpenAPI document.
pros: Understood by everyone and every tool
cons: Clients may need several calls for one screen
guide: Name resources and their operations
Write or generate the OpenAPI document
Return consistent error shapes

options.name: GraphQL
options.summary: One endpoint; clients ask for exactly the data they need.
pros: Clients fetch exactly what a screen needs
cons: Caching and rate limiting are harder
guide: Design the schema first
Add query depth and cost limits
Batch database access (DataLoader)

options.name: gRPC
options.summary: Typed, binary calls between services.
guide: Define services in .proto files
Generate clients and servers
Add deadlines and retries
